en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Defeats (Pārājika-khaṇḍa)
1. The First Pārājika Training Rule Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Verañjā Chapter
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree together with a large Saṅgha of monks, numbering about five hundred monks.
The brahmin of Verañjā heard:

"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is staying at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree together with a large Saṅgha of monks, numbering about five hundred monks."
Furthermore, this good report has spread concerning the venerable Gotama:

"Truly, that Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin of Verañjā approached the Blessed One; having approached, [he stood] together with the Blessed One.
He exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the brahmin of Verañjā said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard this, Master Gotama:"

‘The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of their journey, and reached the final stage of life; nor does he rise up for them, or invite them to a seat.

Is this indeed so, Master Gotama? Does Master Gotama not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the end of their journey, and reached the final stage of life, nor rise up for them, nor invite them to a seat?
This, Master Gotama, is certainly not proper.”

“Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, whom I should honor, rise for, or invite to a seat.
For if the Tathāgata were to honor, rise for, or invite anyone to a seat, his head would split asunder.
“Master Gotama is devoid of flavor,” [the brahmin said].
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is devoid of flavor.

For those flavors of forms, flavors of sounds, flavors of odors, flavors of tastes, and flavors of tangibles that exist, brahmin, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking correctly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is without taste,’ yet it is not with reference to what you have said.
“Master Gotama has no enjoyment?
“There is indeed, brahmin, a way in which one speaking correctly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama has no enjoyment.’”

“Those enjoyments of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects that you have, brahmin, have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.
This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is without enjoyment,’ though it is not with reference to what you have in mind.
“Does Master Gotama advocate the doctrine of non-action?”
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action.
For I, brahmin, advocate non-action regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct;
I advocate non-action regarding manifold evil, unwholesome states.”
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking correctly might say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action,’ though not in the sense that you have in mind.
“Is Master Gotama an annihilationist?
“There is indeed, brahmin, a way in which one speaking correctly might say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist.’”
“Brahmin, I do indeed speak of the annihilation of lust, hatred, and delusion;
I speak of the annihilation of manifold evil, unwholesome states.
This, brahmin, is the sense in which one speaking rightly could say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.”
“Is Master Gotama one who feels disgust?
“There is indeed a way, brahmin, by which one speaking rightly could say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who feels disgust.
For I, brahmin, feel disgust for bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.”
“I am disgusted by the attainment of manifold evil, unwholesome states.
This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is disgusted,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
“Master Gotama is an eradicator?”
“There is, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a remover.
For I, brahmin, teach the Dhamma for the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion;
I teach the Dhamma for the removal of manifold evil, unwholesome states.”
“Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking correctly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is an extirpator,’ though not in the sense that you have in mind.
“Is Master Gotama an ascetic?
“There is indeed, Brahmin, a way in which one speaking correctly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic.’”
"Brahmin, I call those evil, unwholesome states 'tormenting': bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.

One who has abandoned such tormenting, evil, unwholesome states—cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no longer subject to future arising—I call him an ascetic (*tapassin*).

Brahmin, for the Tathāgata, such tormenting, evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no longer subject to future arising."
“This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic of austerity,’ though not in the sense that you have in mind.
“Is Master Gotama one who avoids the womb?
“There is indeed, brahmin, a way in which one speaking rightly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who avoids the womb.’”

“Brahmin, whoever has abandoned the future lying in a womb, the production of renewed existence, having cut it off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered incapable of future arising, and subject to non-reappearance—I call him ‘one who does not enter a womb.

Brahmin, for the Tathāgata, the future lying in a womb, the production of renewed existence, has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered incapable of future arising, and subject to non-reappearance.”
This, brahmin, is the way in which one speaking rightly might say of me, ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who refrains from procreation,’ but it is not with reference to what you have said.
Suppose, brahmin, there were a hen with eight,
ten, or twelve eggs, which she had properly incubated, properly warmed, and properly nurtured.

“Now, if among those chicks from the hen’s eggs, one were to break open the eggshell first with the tip of its claw or its beak and emerge safely, how should it be called— is it the ‘eldest’ or the ‘youngest’?
“It should be called the ‘eldest,’ Master Gotama.”
“For he is indeed their eldest.

“In the same way, brahmin, for a generation shrouded in ignorance, like one trapped in an egg, I alone have burst through the shell of the egg of ignorance and awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in the world.
Therefore, brahmin, I am the eldest and the most excellent in the world.”
“Moreover, brahmin, my energy was aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness was established and unconfused; my body was tranquil and unagitated; and my mind was concentrated and one-pointed.

Then, brahmin, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; I experienced happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare:
"He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness"; thus I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
I recollected my manifold past lives, that is to say:
One birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births,
forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births,
a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both contraction and expansion.
Regarding the aeons of dissolution and evolution:
"In such-and-such a place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose in another place."
"There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus I recollect my manifold past lives in their modes and details.
This, brahmin, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night:
ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose;
darkness was dispelled, light arose—for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“This, brahmin, was my first breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understood how beings fare according to their kamma.”

‘Indeed, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind; they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.’
‘But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking kamma based on right view—
upon the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye,

purified and surpassing that of humans, I see beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and I understand how beings fare according to their kamma.
This, brahmin, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night:
ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose;
darkness was dispelled, light arose—just as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“This, brahmin, was my second breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’”
I directly knew, “This is the cessation of suffering,” as it truly is; I directly knew, “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,” as it truly is;
I directly knew, “These are the taints,” as they truly are; I directly knew, “This is the origin of the taints,” as it truly is.
‘This is the cessation of the taints,’ I directly knew as it really is; ‘this is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints,’ I directly knew as it really is.
As I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of existence, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When I was liberated, the knowledge arose: "It is liberated.
I directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, brahmin, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night.
“Ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose;
darkness was dispelled and light arose—just as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
This, brahmin, was my third breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell.”
When this was said, the brahmin of Verañjā said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama is the eldest; Master Gotama is the most excellent.
Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!”

"Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
And may Master Gotama consent to spend the rains retreat at Verañjā together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the brahmin of Verañjā, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Now at that time, Verañjā was suffering from a famine—food was scarce, crops were withered and bleached, and people lived by gleaning ears of grain; it was not easy to subsist by gathering gleanings.
At that same time, horse-dealers from the northern regions had arrived in Verañjā for the rainy-season residence with about five hundred horses.
In those garden enclosures, a layer of husks had been spread out for the bhikkhus.
In the morning, the bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Verañjā for alms;
not obtaining alms there, they wandered for alms within the garden enclosures and, having brought the husks back to the monastery, [placed them] upon the mortar.
They used it by pounding it again and again.
However, the Venerable Ānanda would grind fresh rice-porridge on a stone and offer it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One would consume it.
Then, the Blessed One heard the sound of the mortar.
Tathāgatas ask even when they know; they do not ask even when they know.
Having discerned the right time, they ask; having discerned the right time, they do not ask.
Tathāgatas ask what is connected with the goal, not what is not connected with the goal.
The destruction of the bridge for those who have acted for their own harm is characteristic of the Tathāgatas.
In two ways do the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, question the bhikkhus: either "We shall teach the Dhamma," or "We shall lay down a training rule for the disciples.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is that sound of a mortar?"
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
You, Ānanda, are true men who have conquered. Future generations will hold rice and meat-rice in contempt.”
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
"At present, Bhante, Verañjā is short of food, with crops blighted by drought, reduced to skeletons, and subsisting on sticks."
"It is not easy to subsist by gleaning or by gathering.
Venerable sir, the lower surface of this great earth is as full of essence as if it were pure, dark honey; such is its flavor.
Venerable sir, I could turn the earth over so that the monks might enjoy the sap of the fungi."
“But as for those living beings, Moggallāna, who depend on the earth—how will you deal with them?
“Venerable sir, I shall manifest a single hand just like the great earth. I shall transfer those living beings who depend on the earth there.
With one hand, I shall turn over the earth.”
“Enough, Moggallāna; do not let it please you to overturn the earth.
Beings might even suffer from such a disorientation.
“Excellent, Bhante! Let the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus go to Uttarakuru for alms.”
“Enough, Moggallāna, let it not be pleasing to you that the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus should go to Uttarakuru for alms.
Then, while the Venerable Sāriputta was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Of which Blessed Buddhas did the holy life not endure for long?”
“Of which Buddhas, Blessed Ones, was the holy life long-lasting?
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind:
‘Of which Blessed Buddhas did the holy life not endure for long? Of which [Buddhas]…’”
“The holy life of the Blessed Buddhas has endured for a long time.
“Venerable sir, of which Blessed Buddhas did the holy life not endure for a long time,
and of which Blessed Buddhas did the holy life endure for a long time?”
“Sāriputta, the holy life under the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū did not endure for long.
But, Sāriputta, the holy life under the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa did endure for long.”
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the holy life under the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū did not endure for long?
“Sāriputta, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū were weary of teaching the Dhamma in detail to their disciples.
And there was little of them—sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla.”
The training rule for disciples had not been laid down; the Pātimokkha had not been recited.

With the disappearance of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and with the disappearance of the disciples who had awakened under them, those final disciples—of various names, various clans, various births, and various families who had gone forth—[abandoned] that holy life.
They quickly vanished. Just as, Sāriputta,
various flowers placed on a board, not held together by a string, are scattered, dispersed, and destroyed by the wind—
for what reason is that?
Just as [they are] not included in that Sutta,
even so, Sāriputta, with the disappearance of those Blessed Buddhas and the disappearance of their disciples who were enlightened after the Buddha (buddhānubuddha),
there arose those final disciples of various names, various clans, various births, and various families.
Those who had gone forth quickly caused that holy life to disappear.
And those Blessed Ones were untiring in exhorting their disciples by encompassing their minds with their own minds.

Once upon a time, Sāriputta, the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was in a certain terrifying forest thicket, exhorting and instructing a Saṅgha of one thousand bhikkhus by encompassing their minds with his own mind.
‘Think in this way, do not think in that way;
attend to the mind in this way, do not attend to it in that way;
abandon this, and having entered upon this, dwell therein.’

Then, Sāriputta, as that thousand of bhikkhus was being thus exhorted and instructed by the Blessed One Vessabhū, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, their minds were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

Therein, Sāriputta, in that terrifying forest thicket, it was truly terrifying: whoever entered that forest thicket who had not yet overcome passion would, for the most part, have his hair stand on end.
“This, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the reason why the holy life under the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū did not endure for long.
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason why the holy life under the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa did endure for long?”
“Sāriputta, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa were not weary of teaching the Dhamma in detail to their disciples.
They had much Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla;
they had laid down training rules for their disciples and recited the Pātimokkha.”
With the disappearance of those Blessed Buddhas and with the disappearance of their disciples who had awakened after the Buddhas,
those final disciples— of various names, various clans, various births, and various families who had gone forth—
maintained that holy life for a long time, throughout a vast period.
Just as, Sāriputta, various flowers placed on a board and well-fastened together with a string are not scattered, dispersed, or destroyed by the wind—
for what reason?
Because they are well-fastened together with the string.
In the same way, Sāriputta, with the disappearance of those Blessed Buddhas and the disappearance of their disciples who had awakened after the Buddha,
those final disciples— of various names, various clans, various births, and various families who had gone forth—
established that holy life for a long time, for a very long period.
“This, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the reason why the holy life of the Blessed One Kakusandha, of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and of the Blessed One Kassapa endured for a long time.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said to him:
“This is the time, Blessed One; this is the time, Sugata.”
“The training rule that the Blessed One would prescribe for his disciples and recite as the Pātimokkha, so that this holy life might endure and last for a long time.
“Wait, Sāriputta! Wait, Sāriputta!
Only the Tathāgata knows the proper time for that.”

“Sāriputta, the Teacher does not lay down training rules for his disciples or recite the Pātimokkha as long as certain conditions conducive to the arising of taints do not appear among the Saṅgha. But when, Sāriputta,
such conditions conducive to the arising of taints do appear among the Saṅgha, then the Teacher lays down training rules for his disciples.”
He recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those very things that are the basis for the taints.
Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not attained the greatness of seniority, certain things that are the basis for the taints do not appear here within the Saṅgha.
But when, Sāriputta, the Saṅgha has attained the greatness of seniority, then certain things that are the basis for the taints appear here within the Saṅgha.

When certain conditions conducive to the influxes (*āsava*) become manifest in the Saṅgha, then the Teacher prescribes a training rule for his disciples and recites the Pātimokkha for the purpose of warding off those very conditions conducive to the influxes. But,
Sāriputta, these conditions conducive to the influxes do not yet become manifest here in the Saṅgha as long as the Saṅgha has not reached great expansion and abundance.
But when, Sāriputta, the Saṅgha has reached great expansion and magnitude, then certain things that are bases for the influxes (āsava) manifest within the Saṅgha;
then the Teacher lays down a training rule and recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those very same things that are bases for the influxes.
“Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not attained the pinnacle of gain and greatness, certain conditions conducive to the arising of taints do not appear within the Saṅgha.
But when the Saṅgha has attained the pinnacle of gain and greatness, then certain conditions conducive to the arising of taints appear within the Saṅgha;
it is then that the Teacher lays down and proclaims a training rule for his disciples.”
The Pātimokkha is for the purpose of warding off those very things that are the basis for the taints.
Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not attained greatness in learning, certain things that are the basis for the taints do not appear here within the Saṅgha.
But when, Sāriputta, the Saṅgha has attained greatness in learning, then certain things that are the basis for the taints appear here within the Saṅgha.
The phenomena appear within the Saṅgha, and then the Teacher prescribes a training rule and recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those very phenomena that are the basis for the taints.
For, Sāriputta, the Bhikkhu Saṅgha is free from corruption, free from danger, devoid of black qualities, pure, and established in the essence.
“Sāriputta, among these five hundred bhikkhus, even the one who is the least is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, it is the custom of the Tathāgatas that when they have been invited to spend the rains retreat, they do not set out on a journey through the countryside without taking leave of those people.
Come, Ānanda, let us take leave of the brahmin of Verañjā.”
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, approached the residence of the brahmin of Verañjā. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin of Verañjā approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As the brahmin of Verañjā was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “We have been invited by you, brahmin, and having completed the rains retreat, we seek your leave, saying:
‘We wish to set out on a wandering tour of the countryside.
“It is true, Master Gotama, that I invited you after you had completed the rains retreat; however, the gift to be given has not yet been bestowed.”
"But that is not because it does not exist, nor is it because of a desire not to give; for how could it be obtained here, when household life has many duties and many tasks?
May the venerable Gotama, together with the community of monks, accept a meal from me tomorrow."
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the brahmin of Verañjā with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.

Then, at the end of that night, the brahmin of Verañjā had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own residence and had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.”

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the brahmin Verañja. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then the brahmin Verañja, with his own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, [the brahmin] [honored him] with the three robes.
He covered [the ground], and he clothed each individual monk with a pair of garments.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmin Verañja with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Verañjā for as long as he pleased, proceeded to Soreyya and Saṅkassa.
He went from Kaṇṇakujja to the place where the Ganges meets the plains;
having arrived there, he crossed the river Ganges at Payāgapatiṭṭhāna and proceeded toward Bārāṇasī.
Then, after staying in Bārāṇasī for as long as he pleased, the Blessed One set out on a wandering tour toward Vesālī.
Wandering by stages on his tour, he arrived at Vesālī.
There, indeed, the Blessed One stayed at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
The section concerning Verañjā is finished.
The First Pārājika Training Rule. 1.
The Section on Sudinna.
Now at that time, not far from Vesālī, there was a village called Kalandagāma. There lived a son of a guild-president named Sudinna, the son of the Kalandas.
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta went to Vesālī with several companions on some business.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated, surrounded by a large assembly, teaching the Dhamma.
Sudinna Kalandaputta saw the Blessed One seated, surrounded by a large assembly, teaching the Dhamma. Upon seeing him, it occurred to him: “What if I were also to listen to the Dhamma?”
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta approached that assembly; having approached, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, this thought occurred to Sudinna Kalandaputta:

“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to practice the holy life in its complete perfection, in its complete purity, polished like a conch shell.”
"What if I were now to shave off my hair and beard, don yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?

Then that assembly, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and departed.
Not long after the assembly had left, Sudinna Kalandaputta approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, Sudinna Kalandaputta said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life, utterly perfect and pure, polished like a conch shell.
“Venerable sir, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
May the Blessed One let me go forth.
“But have you been permitted by your mother and father, Sudinna, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?”
“Venerable sir, I have not been permitted by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Sudinna, the Tathāgatas do not allow a son to go forth who has not been permitted by his parents.
“Venerable sir, I shall act in such a way that my parents will permit me to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta, having completed his business in Vesālī, went to the village of Kalandaka where his parents were; having approached them, he said this to his parents:

"Mother and father, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life in its complete perfection, in its complete purity, polished like a conch shell."
“I wish, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned saffron robes, to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Please grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
When this was said, Sudinna Kalandaputta’s mother and father spoke thus to Sudinna Kalandaputta:
“Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, beloved and dear, raised in comfort and brought up in luxury. You, dear Sudinna, know nothing of suffering.
Even at your death we would be unwillingly separated from you;
how much less shall we grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living?”
A second time, Sudinna Kalandaputta said this to his mother and father:
“Mother and father, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life in its complete perfection, total purity, and polished fullness.
I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
A second time, Sudinna’s parents said this to him:
“Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, beloved and dear, raised in comfort and brought up in luxury.”
"My dear Sudinna, you know nothing of suffering.
Even at your death we would be parted from you against our will;
how much less shall we give you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living?"
A third time, Sudinna Kalandaputta said this to his mother and father:

“Mother and father, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life in its complete perfection, in its total purity, polished like a conch shell.
I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For a third time, Sudinna’s mother and father said this to Sudinna Kalandaputta:
“Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, beloved and dear, raised in comfort and pampered with ease.”
"My dear Sudinna, you know nothing of suffering.
Even at your death we would be separated from you against our will;
how much more so, while you are still living, could we ever grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness?"
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta, thinking, "My parents do not permit me to go forth from the home life into homelessness," lay down right there on the bare ground,
thinking: "Right here shall be my death, or my going forth."
Then Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, did not eat even one meal; he did not eat two meals;
he did not eat three meals; he did not eat four meals; he did not eat five meals; he did not eat six meals; he did not eat even seven meals.
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta’s mother and father said this to him: “Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, beloved and dear, raised in comfort and nurtured in comfort.
You know nothing, dear Sudinna, of suffering.
Even at your death we would be separated from you against our will.”
"But how could we ever permit him to go forth from the home life into homelessness while he is still living?
Get up, dear Sudinna! Eat and drink and enjoy yourself;
while eating, drinking, and enjoying yourself, delighting in sensual pleasures and performing meritorious deeds, may you find joy."
“We do not grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
When this was said, Sudinna Kalandaputta became silent.
A second time also... [and so on].
A third time, Sudinna Kalandaputta’s mother and father said this to him:
“Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, beloved and dear, raised in comfort and pampered in comfort.
You do not know anything of suffering, dear Sudinna.”
"Even by death we shall be separated from you against our will;
how much more so would we allow you, while you are still living, to go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Rise up, dear Sudinna! Eat, drink, and enjoy yourself!"
“Enjoying yourself, drinking, attending to pleasures, indulging in sensual desires, and performing meritorious deeds—may you take delight in these.
We do not permit you to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
For a third time, Sudinna Kalandaputta remained silent.
Then the companions of Sudinna Kalandaputta approached Sudinna Kalandaputta; having approached him, they said this to Sudinna Kalandaputta:
"Friend Sudinna, you are your mother and father’s only son—dear, beloved, raised in comfort, and pampered in comfort.
You, friend Sudinna, know nothing of suffering."
Even through death your parents will eventually be separated from you against their will;
how much less will they grant you permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness while you are still living?
Arise, dear Sudinna, eat, drink, and enjoy yourself!
“Enjoying yourself, drinking, attending to pleasures, indulging in sensual desires, and performing meritorious deeds—take your delight in these;
your mother and father will not permit you to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
When this was said, Sudinna Kalandaputta remained silent.
A second time...
and a third time, Sudinna’s friends said this to Sudinna Kalandaputta:
"Friend Sudinna, you are indeed... [as before]..."
A third time, Sudinna Kalandaputta remained silent.
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta’s friends went to where his mother and father were; having approached them, they said this to Sudinna Kalandaputta’s mother and father:
“Mother and father, here is Sudinna lying on the bare ground.”
‘Right here my death will occur, or else my going forth.
If you do not grant Sudinna permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness, his death will come upon him right there.
But if you grant Sudinna permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness, you will see him even once he has gone forth.
“If Sudinna does not find delight in going forth from the home life into homelessness, what other destination could there be for him? He will surely return right here.
Grant permission for Sudinna to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“We grant permission, dear ones, for Sudinna to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta’s friends approached him and, having approached, said this to Sudinna Kalandaputta:
“Get up, friend Sudinna! You have been permitted by your mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness.

Then Sudinna Kalandaputta, thinking, “I have indeed been permitted by my mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness,” rose up, joyful and elated, rubbing his limbs with his hand.
Then Sudinna Kalandaputta, having regained his strength after a few days, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, Sudinna Kalandaputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have been permitted by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
May the Blessed One grant me the going forth.
Sudinna Kalandaputta received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.

Not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Sudinna undertook and practiced such ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa): he was a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a wearer of rag-robes, and one who went for alms from house to house in regular order.
He lived in dependence on a certain village of the Vajjis.

Now at that time, the Vajjis were suffering from a famine; it was a time of scarcity, with crops blighted by drought and turned to white stalks, so that they had to subsist by gleaning ears of grain. It was not easy to maintain oneself by gathering gleanings.

Then it occurred to the Venerable Sudinna: “At present, the Vajjis are suffering from famine; there is a scarcity of food, crops have withered, bones are bleached white, and people subsist by gleaning ears of grain. It is not easy to maintain oneself by gathering gleanings.
Now, I have many kinsmen in Vesālī who are wealthy, affluent, and opulent, possessing abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and equipment, and abundant wealth and grain.
What if I were to live depending on my kinsmen?”
“Relying on my kinsmen, they will give gifts and perform meritorious deeds; the monks will receive gains, and I too shall not go hungry for alms.
Then the Venerable Sudinna, having put away his bedding and taking his bowl and robe, set out for Vesālī.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Vesālī. There, the Venerable Sudinna dwelt in Vesālī at the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.

The relatives of the Venerable Sudinna heard that “Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, has indeed arrived at Vesālī. They brought a gift of food consisting of sixty measures of cooked rice to the Venerable Sudinna.
Then the Venerable Sudinna, having distributed those sixty measures of cooked rice among the monks, dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered the village of Kalandaka for alms.
While walking for alms from house to house in the village of Kalandaka, he approached his own father’s residence.
Now at that time, the female slave of the Venerable Sudinna’s relatives was wishing to throw away some porridge from the previous evening.
Then the Venerable Sudinna said this to that female slave:
“Sister, if it is something fit to be thrown away, pour it here into my bowl.”
Then, as the female slave of Venerable Sudinna’s relatives was pouring that overnight porridge into Venerable Sudinna’s bowl, she observed the marks of his hands, feet, and voice.
Thereupon, the female slave of Venerable Sudinna’s relatives went to Venerable Sudinna’s mother; having approached her, she said this to Venerable Sudinna’s mother:
“O lady, you should know this.”
“Master’s son Sudinna has arrived.
“If you speak the truth, my girl, I shall make you a slave,” he said.
At that time, the Venerable Sudinna was eating that overnight sour gruel leaning against the base of a certain wall.
The father, too, while returning from his own work, saw the Venerable Sudinna eating that overnight sour gruel leaning against the base of a certain wall.
Having seen him, he approached the Venerable Sudinna and said to him:
"My dear Sudinna, you actually eat such overnight sour gruel?"
“Indeed, dear Sudinna, you ought to go to your own home.
“We have already been to your home, householder;
this is the porridge from last night.”
Then the Venerable Sudinna’s father, taking the Venerable Sudinna by the arm, said this to him: “Come, dear Sudinna, let us go home.
Then the Venerable Sudinna went to his own father’s residence; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the Venerable Sudinna’s father said this to the Venerable Sudinna: “Eat, dear Sudinna.”
“Enough, householder; my meal for today is finished.
“Please accept tomorrow’s meal, dear Sudinna,” he said.
The Venerable Sudinna consented by remaining silent. Then the Venerable Sudinna rose from his seat and departed.
Then, when that night had passed, the venerable Sudinna’s mother had the ground smeared with fresh cow dung and had two heaps made—one of silver and one of gold.
Those heaps were so vast that a man standing on this side could not see a man standing on the other side, nor could a man standing on the other side see a man standing on this side.
Having had those heaps covered with mats, having prepared a seat in the middle, and having surrounded it with a curtain, she addressed the venerable Sudinna’s former wife:
“Now then, daughter-in-law, adorn yourself with that same jewelry with which you were adorned when you were dear and pleasing to my son Sudinna.
“Very well, noble lady,” the venerable Sudinna’s former wife replied to the venerable Sudinna’s mother.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sudinna dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to his father’s house. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the Venerable Sudinna’s father approached the Venerable Sudinna; having approached, he had those heaps uncovered and said this to the Venerable Sudinna:
“This, dear Sudinna, is your mother’s wealth in women—a woman for a woman; one part from your paternal line, and another from your grandfather’s.”
“It is possible, dear Sudinna, to return to the lower life in order to enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds.
Come, dear Sudinna, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
“Father, I am not able, I am not strong enough; I am delighted as I lead the holy life.”
A second time...
and a third time, the venerable Sudinna’s father said this to the venerable Sudinna:
“This, dear Sudinna, is your mother’s clay [inheritance], a woman’s woman-wealth; some is from your father, and some from your grandfather.”
“It is possible, dear Sudinna, for you to return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
Come, dear Sudinna, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
“We would say that to you, householder, if you would not press us so hard.”
“Go then, dear Sudinna.
“In that case, householder, have large hemp-sacks made, fill them with gold and bullion, have them transported by carts, and cast them into the middle of the Ganges’ current.
Why is that? Because—”
“For whatever fear, trepidation, horripilation, or need for protection you might have on that account, householder, that shall not happen to you.
When this was said, the venerable Sudinna’s father became displeased, thinking, “How can my son Sudinna speak thus?
Then the venerable Sudinna’s father addressed the venerable Sudinna’s former wife:
“In that case, my dear, you are beloved and pleasing. Perhaps even our son Sudinna might do as you say.
Then the former wife of the Venerable Sudinna took hold of the Venerable Sudinna’s feet and said to him:
“My lord’s son, what kind of nymphs are they for whose sake you lead the holy life?”
“I do not, sister, lead the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs.
Then the venerable Sudinna’s former wife, thinking, “From this day forward, Master Sudinna addresses me by the title ‘sister,’” fainted right there and fell down.
Then the venerable Sudinna said this to his father:
“If, householder, food is to be given, give it;
do not cause us distress.
“Eat, dear Sudinna,” he said.
Then the venerable Sudinna’s mother and father personally served and satisfied the venerable Sudinna with various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft.
Then, when the venerable Sudinna had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, his mother said this to him:
“Dear Sudinna, this family is wealthy, of great riches and great possessions, with abundant gold and silver, abundant wealth and equipment, and abundant money and grain.”
“It is possible, dear Sudinna, to return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
Come, dear Sudinna, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
“Mother, I am not able, I am not capable; I am delighted as I lead the holy life.”
A second time...
and a third time, the venerable Sudinna’s mother said this to the venerable Sudinna:
“Dear Sudinna, this family is wealthy, of great riches and great possessions; it has abundant gold and silver, abundant wealth and equipment, and abundant money and grain.”
"In that case, dear Sudinna, give us even a seed,
lest the Licchavis confiscate our property on the grounds that we are childless.
"I can do that, mother," he replied.
“But where, dear Sudinna, are you staying now?
“In the Great Forest, mother,” he replied.
Then the Venerable Sudinna rose from his seat and departed.
Then the venerable Sudinna’s mother addressed his former wife:
“In that case, my daughter-in-law, whenever you are in season and your menses have appeared, you should inform me.
“Very well, noble lady,” the venerable Sudinna’s former wife replied to the venerable Sudinna’s mother.
Then, before long, the venerable Sudinna’s former wife became subject to her season; her menses appeared.
Then the venerable Sudinna’s former wife said this to the venerable Sudinna’s mother: “I am subject to my season, noble lady;
my menses have appeared. “In that case, daughter-in-law, adorn yourself with whatever ornaments made you dear and pleasing to your son Sudinna.”
“Yes, noble lady,” the former wife of the Venerable Sudinna replied to the Venerable Sudinna’s mother.
Then the Venerable Sudinna’s mother, taking his former wife with her, went to the Great Wood where the Venerable Sudinna was staying. Having approached him, she said this to the Venerable Sudinna:
“Dear Sudinna, this family is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; it has abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and requisites, and abundant wealth and grain.”
“It is possible, dear Sudinna, to turn back to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
Come, dear Sudinna, turn back to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.
“Mother, I am not able; I am not strong enough.”
“Delighted, I am living the holy life.
A second time… and a third time,
the Venerable Sudinna’s mother said this to the Venerable Sudinna:
“Dear Sudinna, this family is wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments; it has abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and requisites, and abundant wealth and grain.
Therefore, dear Sudinna, give them even a seed—let the Licchavis not seize our inheritance on the grounds that we are childless.”
“Mother, I can certainly do that,” he said.

Taking his former wife by the arm, he led her deep into the Great Forest; and since he did not perceive the danger in what was not yet a formulated training rule, he solicited sexual intercourse from his former wife three times.
She consequently conceived a child.
The earth-dwelling deities raised a cry:
"Alas, friends! The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is indeed free from corruption and free from danger;
yet Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, has brought about corruption, he has brought about danger!"
Having heard the sound of the earth-dwelling deities, the Cātumahārājika deities raised a cry...
[and so on] ...the Tāvatiṃsa deities...
the Yāma deities...
the Tusita devas … the Nimmānarati devas … the Paranimmitavasavatti devas …
The deities of the Brahma-world raised a cry:
"Alas, sirs! The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is indeed free from corruption and free from danger;
yet Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, has introduced corruption, he has introduced danger!"
At that very moment, at that very instant, the sound rose up as far as the Brahma-world.
Then, as the pregnancy reached its full term, the venerable Sudinna’s former wife gave birth to a son.
Thereupon, the venerable Sudinna’s companions gave the boy the name Bījaka.
They gave the name Bījakamātā to the former wife of the Venerable Sudinna,
and they gave the name Bījakapitā to the Venerable Sudinna.
At a later time, both of them went forth from the household life into homelessness and realized arhatship.
Then, indeed, remorse arose in the Venerable Sudinna, and he felt regret:
"It is a loss for me, truly not a gain;
it is ill-gained by me, truly not well-gained, that having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, I was unable to lead the holy life perfectly and purely for as long as life lasts."
Because of that very anxiety and remorse, he became thin, wretched, discolored, and pale, with veins showing all over his body; dejected, depressed, suffering, and unhappy, he brooded in remorse.
Then the bhikkhus who were friends of the Venerable Sudinna said to him:
"Formerly, friend Sudinna, you were handsome, with bright faculties, a serene complexion, and a clear skin tone."
“Now at present you are thin, wretched, discolored, jaundiced, with veins protruding all over your body; you are dejected in mind, depressed in mind, suffering, unhappy, remorseful, and brooding.
I wonder, friend Sudinna, whether you are leading the holy life without being content?
“I am not, friend, leading the holy life without being content.”
"I have committed an evil deed:
I engaged in sexual intercourse with my former wife.
Because of this, friends, remorse arose within me and I felt regret."
“Alas, it is a loss for me! Truly, it is not a gain for me! Alas, it is ill-gained by me! Truly, it is not well-gained by me!
For although I have gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, I was unable to live the complete and pure holy life for as long as I lived.”

“Enough, friend Sudinna, of remorse and enough of regret, since you, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, will not be able to lead the holy life completely and purely for as long as life lasts.
Has not the Dhamma been taught by the Blessed One in many ways for dispassion, not for passion;
for detachment, not for bondage?”
The Dhamma has been taught for non-clinging, not for clinging.

In this regard, friend, while the Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One for dispassion, you would direct your mind toward passion; while the Dhamma has been taught for disentanglement, you would direct your mind toward bondage; while the Dhamma has been taught for non-clinging, you would direct your mind toward clinging.
Is it not true, friend, that the Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One in many ways for the fading away of passion?

The Dhamma has been taught for the purpose of intoxication-free exhilaration, for the removal of thirst, for the uprooting of attachment, for the cutting off of the cycle of existence, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation,
and for Nibbāna. Surely, friends, in many ways the Blessed One has declared the abandoning of sensual pleasures and the full understanding of perceptions of sensual pleasure.
The removal of thirst for sensual pleasures has been declared;
the eradication of sensual thoughts has been declared;
the calming of the fever of sensual pleasures has been declared.
“Friends, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence, nor to the increase of the confidence of those who already have it.
On the contrary, friends, this leads to the lack of confidence in those without confidence, and to the alienation of some among those who have confidence.
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Sudinna in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the Venerable Sudinna:
“Is it true, Sudinna, that you have engaged in sexual intercourse with your former wife?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unseemly, foolish man, it is unbecoming, it is unsuitable, it is unworthy of a recluse, it is improper, and it is not to be done.
How can you, foolish man, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, be unable to live the complete and pure holy life for as long as you live?”
"Have I not, O foolish man, taught the Dhamma in many ways for dispassion, not for passion;
for detachment, not for bondage;
for non-clinging, not for clinging?"

"In that case, you foolish man, when I have taught the Dhamma for the sake of dispassion, you will direct your mind toward passion; when I have taught the Dhamma for the sake of disentanglement, you will direct your mind toward bondage; when I have taught the Dhamma for the sake of non-clinging, you will direct your mind toward clinging.
Have I not, foolish man, taught the Dhamma in many ways for the fading away of passion?

I have taught the Dhamma for the intoxication-freeing of pride, for the removal of thirst, for the uprooting of attachment, for the cutting off of the round of existence, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, and for Nibbāna."
"Have I not, O foolish man, in many ways declared the abandoning of sensual pleasures,
declared the full understanding of perceptions of sensual pleasure,
and declared the removal of thirst for sensual pleasure?"
The eradication of thoughts of sensual desire has been declared;
the subsiding of the fever of sensual desire has been declared.
It would be better for you, foolish man, that your genitals be thrust into the mouth of a fierce venomous snake, than that your genitals be thrust into the genitals of a woman.
"It would be better for you, foolish man, that your penis be thrust into the mouth of a black snake than that it be thrust into the female organ of a woman.

It would be better for you, foolish man, that your penis be thrust into a pit of glowing embers, aflame, blazing, and radiant, than that it be thrust into the female organ of a woman. And why is that?"

For on that account, foolish man, one might meet death or experience suffering amounting to death; yet for that reason alone, upon the breakup of the body after death, one would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
But on this account, foolish man, upon the breakup of the body after death, one would indeed be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
In this matter, you fool, that you would engage in unrighteousness, the village custom, the practice of outcasts, lewdness, the water-edge rite, secrecy, and sexual intercourse— since you, fool,
are the originator and leader of many unwholesome states—
this will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence, nor to the increase of the confidence of those who already have it.
“Thus, foolish man, this will lead to the lack of confidence in those who have no confidence, and to the alienation of some of those who are already confident.

Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the Venerable Sudinna in many ways, spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support, difficult to maintain, of great desire, of lack of contentment, of socializing, and of laziness; and having spoken in many ways, [he addressed the monks:]
Having spoken in praise of being easy to support, easy to satisfy, of fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, the ascetic qualities,
inspiring confidence, reduction of burdens, and the arousal of energy,
and having given the monks a Dhamma talk appropriate and conducive thereto, he addressed the monks:
“Therefore, monks, for ten reasons I shall lay down a training rule for the monks:
for the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the ease of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of ill-behaved persons, for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved monks,
for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives.”
For the inspiring of those without faith, for the increase of those with faith, for the stability of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whosoever bhikkhu should engage in sexual intercourse, he is defeated and no longer in communion."
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
The section concerning Sudinna is finished.
2. The Story of the Female Monkey.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu in the Great Wood at Vesālī had lured a female monkey with food and was engaging in sexual intercourse with her.
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, that bhikkhu entered Vesālī for alms.
At that time, several bhikkhus, while wandering about the dwellings, approached the dwelling of that bhikkhu.
That female monkey saw those monks coming from afar.
Having seen them, she approached them; having approached, she wagged her buttocks in front of those monks, wagged her tail, spread her buttocks, and made a sign.
Then it occurred to those monks: “Without a doubt, that monk is engaging in sexual intercourse with this female monkey. They hid themselves to one side.
Then that bhikkhu, having walked for alms in Vesālī and taken his almsfood, returned.
Then that female monkey approached that bhikkhu.
Thereupon, that bhikkhu ate a portion of that almsfood and gave a portion to the female monkey.
